name: Paragonimus spp.

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: P. westermani eggs: approximately 80–120 × 45–70 µm, golden-brown, thick shell, operculum and asymmetric profile with opposite-end thickening.
Other Paragonimus species differ in dimensions; eggs are unembryonated when released.

transmission.detail: Snail stages infect crabs or crayfish; ingested metacercariae migrate to the lungs, with possible ectopic migration.

life_cycle.detail: Snail stages infect crabs or crayfish; ingested metacercariae migrate to the lungs, with possible ectopic migration.
Eggs in sputum or swallowed eggs in stool; specimen origin must accompany image labels.

hosts: Definitive: humans and carnivorous mammals. Intermediate: snail then freshwater crustacean.
distribution: Species occur in Asia, Africa and the Americas. P. heterotremus is particularly relevant to Thailand and neighboring countries.
clinical_significance: Chronic cough, blood-stained sputum and chest disease can mimic tuberculosis; ectopic brain infection can cause neurological disease.
specimen: Eggs in sputum or swallowed eggs in stool; specimen origin must accompany image labels.
diagnostics: Microscopy of sputum and stool at 100–400×; serology can assist when eggs are absent.
differential_diagnosis: Distinguish from other large operculated eggs using specimen origin and morphology; genus-level eggs do not confirm P. westermani.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
